title: Latency Storm Mitigation and KV-Cache Repopulation with Lumen Health
summary: Deep dive on strategies to avoid 'latency storms' during traffic spikes: prioritized queueing, KV-cache repopulation patterns, and reserved GPU sizing with burst policies. Discussed on-prem VPC constraints, quantization trade-offs for tail latency, and concrete microbenchmarks the customer will run. Agreed next steps include an SLO mapping doc, a short benchmark plan, and a pilot config for a limited canary pool.
topics: KV cache warmup and repopulation strategies
burst and backpressure: priority queues, token-bucket shaping
reserved GPU sizing and prewarmed pool strategies
quantization impact on latency variance and throughput
VPC / on-prem networking constraints and egress limits
benchmarks and pilot plan for Lumen's summarization workload
transcript:
00:00 Tara (Redwood AE): okay everyone thanks for carving out time today, um the goal is to walk through what we called a latency storm mitigation pattern and then tie that to k v cache repopulation and reserved pool sizing. we have about 55 minutes. uh quick intros?
00:18 Carlos (Lumen): yeah carlos here, ml infra, we run summarization and clinical note gen at peak hours, and the tail latency right now is our biggest fear.
00:27 Priya (Lumen): priya - platform, mostly network and ops, VPC peering and egress limits are a hard constraint for us.
00:33 Tara: great. julian, want to kick off the technical bits?
00:37 Julian (Redwood SE): sure. so first quick picture: most latency storms we see are because cache misses synchronize. a lot of requests hit same prefix, k v cache is cold, the model starts serving from scratch, and the GPU queue spikes. you get head-of-line blocking.
00:52 Evan (Lumen): "head of line" yep that sounds like our 2am window last month when a batch job triggered and then interactive traffic exploded.
00:58 Julian: exactly. so we recommend a few things: prefix-aware prewarming, prioritized request queues (so interactive requests beat background batch), and a staged fallback to a smaller quantized variant while cache warms.
01:12 Amy (Lumen): smaller variant as in lower-parameter model in the same pool? or run a separate pool?
01:18 Julian: good Q. usually separate pool with pre-warmed quantized weights gives the best trade: you pay slightly for the separate warm pool but it absorbs tails. if you try to run both in the same process you end up with eviction thrash. (uh) also routing policy needs to be traffic-aware.
01:33 Tara: we can also fallback to function-calling style short answers while the heavy model warms, is that something you could accept?
01:38 Carlos: maybe for non-critical endpoints, but clinical summaries have to be high fidelity. we want latency fixes that don't degrade output quality.
01:45 Julian: understood. there's a hybrid pattern: serve a compact summary from quantized model for the first N tokens while k v cache repopulates on the full model, and then stitch or rescoring. this keeps perceived latency low while preserving final quality for long-running workflows.
01:58 Priya: what's the observed extra latency of a repopulation vs a warmed request? like numbers.
02:03 Julian: on our internal benchmarks with a long-context summarization model, a cold request can add 800-1200ms for the first 256 tokens compared to a warm request. with 4-bit quantization the cold-run often is slightly faster per-token but has higher variance and worse quality for some instructions.
02:22 Tara: and that's why we suggest measuring with your real workload — token mix and prompt diversity matters.
02:28 Carlos: ok can we talk about queueing model? we heard someone mention M M c?
02:33 Julian: yeah the quick mental model is an M/M/c with nonstationary arrival rates. the c is your active GPU workers. when arrival rate spikes above c * mu, queue builds — tail blows up fast. we add priority queues and admission control: token-bucket shaping per key, plus a fast-path queue for interactive.
02:48 Evan: token-bucket shaping means we can throttle batch jobs to preserve headroom for interactive?
02:52 Julian: exactly. side note: for reserved pools we allow configurable burst credit so scheduled batch can borrow headroom but with strict payback policy. that prevents runaway consumption.
03:05 Priya: what about prewarming semantics — do you pre-initialize KV caches proactively from hot prefixes?
03:10 Maya (Redwood): we do prefix-aware liveliness checks. for customers we can ingest a hot-prefix list from your telemetry and prepopulate K V cache at pool startup or on a short TTL refresh. There is a trade: large prewarm increases memory footprint and startup time.
03:26 Carlos: our hot-prefix list is messy — many variants from different services. do you support approximate matching?
03:31 Julian: yes, we can do prefix clustering and fuzzy matching heuristics to cover variants without warming every distinct key. that reduces memory by ~30% in our tests.
03:41 Amy: curious about eviction — how do you decide when to evict K V entries? LRU? TTL?
03:46 Julian: combination: priority-based TTL where active prefixes maintain sticky entries, LRU for everything else. customers can pin critical prefixes.
03:55 Evan: networking — when a pool is in a private VPC, prewarming has to happen inside the VPC because we can't egress. is that supported?
04:03 Maya: yes, the Private deployment supports local prewarming during pool init. you provide the keys or we pull from S3 in the same VPC. note there are S3 IAM constraints and startup IAM role implications.
04:14 Priya: also curious about KMS/HSM for key protection during on-prem? we need to keep tokens encrypted at rest.
04:20 Tara: Redwood Private integrates with KMS and can be configured with customer-managed keys; we support HSM for enterprise tiers. we can share the SOC 2 + KMS doc after.
04:30 Carlos: talk me through a sizing calc for reserved GPUs. we currently have two gpus in a pool, and peak concurrency hits 18 req/s with avg 0.6s per token and average tokens 120.
04:41 Julian: rough calc: throughput per GPU = (1 / avg_latency_per_request) * concurrency per request? a simpler approach: profile RPS per GPU with your prompt mix. if you need 18 rps and a warmed GPU gives you ~8 rps for that workload, you'd need 3 GPUs to keep p99 sensible. add one for buffer or enable burst credits.
05:01 Priya: so recommended reserved = 3 + burst buffer?
05:04 Julian: yes, reserved of 3 with a prewarm count of 1 and burst credits that allow spinning ephemeral nodes if the queue rises over threshold.
05:12 Evan: ephemeral spin-up time is like 60-90s? can we rely on that during a storm?
05:17 Julian: ephemeral could take 45-120s depending on infra; that's why we keep pre-warmed ephemeral or a warm standby that costs less. the burst policy does not rely on cold-starts.
05:27 Carlos: ok let's go into quantization tradeoffs — if we quantize to 4-bit we get cost savings but quality issues. does that also change KV cache behavior?
05:35 Julian: quantized variants have smaller KV storage per token due to reduced key sizes but may produce cache patterns that are slightly different, so cache hit rates can change. also decoding throughput per GPU can increase, but tail variance may be worse for some prompts.
05:50 Amy: have you seen cases where quantization improves tail latency consistently?
05:54 Julian: sometimes for pure generation tasks with simple tokenization quantization reduces latency and keeps a tighter distribution. but for instruction-heavy clinical text you may get hallucination risk. our recommendation: A/B test on a holdout set.
06:07 Priya: let's make this concrete — what will Redwood provide as artifacts for our pilot?
06:12 Tara: we'll provide a pilot config: pool sizing recomendation, prewarm script template, a short benchmark harness to run your prompts, and a runbook for burst policies + rollback.
06:22 Carlos: good. also network egress limits mean we can't fetch prewarm payloads from public S3. we'll have to use internal object store.
06:28 Maya: that's fine. we can adapt the prewarm connector to your internal endpoint and we'll need endpoint credentials.
06:34 Evan: on metrics — we need token-level latency, queue depth, cache hit rate, and per-request model variant. can Redwood surface that in the console?
06:42 Tara: yes — per-route dashboards, token-level histograms, and traces. we also produce a CSV/JSON export you can ingest into internal dashboards.
06:50 Carlos: any gotchas with canarying? we plan a 5% canary for the new pool.
06:55 Julian: watch for cold-cache amplification: a small canary that becomes suddenly popular can olfb lead to large misses. for canaries we recommend increasing TTL for pinned prefixes and warm-up the canary pool with a synthetic workload mirroring production distribution.
07:12 Amy: synthetic workload — do you have a generator?
07:15 Maya: we have a small generator and a script that reads a sample of your prompts and replays them at scale. we suggest running 10x multiplexing for 15 minutes to surface tail behaviors.
07:25 Carlos: benchmark plan — can you propose RPS, concurrency, and duration?
07:30 Julian: recommended: ramp to target RPS over 5 minutes, hold for 10 minutes, then spike 3x for 2 minutes to simulate storm. collect p50/p95/p99 latencies and cache hit curves.
07:44 Priya: and error handling — what happens when a request times out during repopulation? do you queue or fail-fast?
07:50 Julian: configurable. we support fail-fast with immediate fallback to a quantized short-answer path, or queue with backpressure. for interactive UI we often prefer fail-fast + graceful degradation.
07:59 Tara: any security concerns on your side we should note?
08:02 Amy: SSO, audit logs, and data residency. we need audit trails of model invocations for compliance.
08:08 Tara: Redwood logs invocation metadata and can push audit logs to your SIEM; we can redact payloads if needed.
08:15 Carlos: ok let's move to a concrete example — here's a scenario: overnight batch churn clears K V cache at 02:00, then at 02:05 interactive traffic surges. what strategy would you pick?
08:27 Julian: first defend interactive traffic: token-bucket to slow batch, prioritized queue for UI requests, and a fast warm standby pool with pinned prefixes. also use synthetic warmers for top-100 prefixes at start-of-window.
08:40 Evan: do we need to change our batch window to avoid overlap?
08:43 Priya: we prefer not to move windows due to upstream dependencies.
08:46 Julian: then rely on admission control and increase burst credits for that window. also mark batch jobs as lower priority so they back off automatically.
08:54 Carlos: curious about costs — does prewarming large caches inflate cost linearly?
08:59 Maya: memory costs increase, and reserved GPUs for warm pools add base cost. however the savings from avoiding large tail latency (lost conversions, SLA penalties) often outweighs the extra footprint. we can model unit economics for your telemetry.
09:12 Amy: unit economics sounds good. can Redwood simulate different reserved sizes quickly?
09:16 Julian: yes we can run capacity simulations using your traffic trace; the tool outputs expected p99 under different pool configs. we'll run that as part of the pilot.
09:25 Tara: let's capture action items and next steps.
09:28 Carlos: quick Q on metrics retention — we need 90 days of traces. is that a paid add-on?
09:33 Tara: yes extended retention is an add-on; we'll include pricing in the follow-up.
09:38 Priya: if we do Private deployment on-prem, are there features missing compared to hosted?
09:43 Maya: mostly telemetry ingestion requires connectors; some managed autoscaling features depend on our control plane. but core runtime features (prefix prewarm, KV caching, prioritized queues) are supported.
09:54 Julian: final note — be careful with aggressive quantization in clinical workflows. do a narrow A/B with clinicians to check for hallucination or correctness drift.
10:05 Tara: ok great. I'm going to summarize next steps and we'll wrap.
10:10 Carlos: thanks all.
